html:
From about 2000 BCE, groups of herders from the steppes north of the Caspian and Aral seas moved south through Central Asia toward Iran and India. They spoke early Indo-Iranian languages, and they brought horses, spoke wheeled chariots and the worship of sky gods.

Their roots lie in the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures of the steppe, with fortified sites like Arkaim. On the way south many passed through the oasis towns of the Oxus civilisation (BMAC) and borrowed words, and perhaps rituals, there. Ancient DNA shows steppe ancestry reaching South Asia between about 2000 and 1500 BCE, carried mostly by men.

One branch, the Indo-Aryans, reached the Punjab after the decline of the Indus cities and composed the Rigveda; their arrival is shown on the chart as the Indo-Aryan migrations. Another branch, the Iranians, settled the Iranian plateau. Around 1400 BCE the Mitanni kings of Syria still swore by Indo-Aryan gods. The movement was a slow drift over centuries, not a single invasion.
